title: The Anointing of the Son in Humanity
english: They treat angels as worthy of worship, yet they pay divine service to the whole creation, even though Scripture declares, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone,' and despite the fact that among us no one has recently claimed to be a god. Perhaps they rush to that common thing, the girl of 378, and say that through union with God, the divine nature according to its own essence is surrounded by glory. Therefore they confess the union is true and do not sophisticate the matter, but instead distinguish the natures and place each part separately, declaring them to be separate from one another. As for the union of persons among us, I do not know how they claim to have discovered it.

Therefore we affirm with confidence concerning the Son who comes from God according to nature and has become as one of us—that is, a man—you have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; for this reason, God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions. This is because the first man transgressed the divine command, and then human nature became exceedingly prone to sin. Therefore, the Logos who comes from God, by nature untrippable, holy, just, and hating injustice, has become as one of us and has been anointed as a servant. He has inscribed God the Father because of the human condition, and yet God as he truly exists; and from him it is said that he is anointed through the Holy Spirit, not receiving this anointing for himself alone.

For he is by nature holy as God. But by his own action he leads us to grace and declares us worthy of the blessing from the Father, although we have long stumbled by the transgression in Adam and by the tyranny of sin that has ruled over us since then.

It was not an elder, nor an angel, but the Lord himself who saved us. Yet if anyone imagines receiving the Word from God the Father into a distinct nature as the sanctification, he will launch himself into a vast ocean of disgrace. For if we claim that the sanctification spoken of here was accomplished in the last times of the age, how can we avoid being compelled, even against our will, to admit that he would not be holy by nature? Indeed, we would have to say he is not holy at all when compared to those who existed from the beginning, before the times of the anointing—those endless ages—and before he came into being, when he shared with us only 379 units of sanctification. And if this is true, then he was not free from sin. How then does the wisest Paul declare that the Son is the radiance of the Father’s glory and the exact imprint of his substance? For the character always reproduces the archetype upon itself. Therefore, the Father himself is not holy by nature. Who, then, sanctifies him? Let those who spoke these things to me be well: we confess that the Son exists by nature as holy, just as we do the Father himself, and we affirm that he was sanctified according to the flesh at the moment when he is said to have emptied himself—having been called a man—in whom, by participation with God and not by his own nature, the sanctification dwells. And it is no surprise that God, being the Word, treats the particularities of humanity with affection and in keeping with the divine economy. For the one who altogether willed to experience the emptying...
...how would he not also sanctify humanity in like manner? But the text breaks off here, leaving the thought incomplete.

title: Divine Anointing
english: The Word from God the Father would not reasonably decline His own things, for if considered in Himself, He is in need of no good, and the Holy Spirit is said to be His own. Since, as I said, He became flesh with His own Spirit, anointing His own temple, the Father works all things through the Son alone in Israel. The Spirit is said to be received economically, as a man, for it is said that Jesus from Nazareth was anointed by God with the Holy Spirit and power (Luke 4:18).

But as God, He gives the Spirit to those worthy to receive it, and indeed, He breathed on the holy apostles, saying 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:22). The divine Peter proclaimed to the Jewish crowds concerning the Spirit, saying that Jesus, having been exalted to the right hand of God, received the promise of the Spirit from the Father and poured it out (Acts 2:33). You hear in these words that He was exalted to the right hand of God, received and gave the Spirit; He was exalted, of course, when He humbled Himself. Just as He willingly humbled Himself for this purpose, so again He exalts Himself, being the hand of the Father by which all things are worked in a godly manner. He is exalted through Himself according to the will of the Father, when, having broken the bonds of death and having said to the spirits below 'Come out' (Luke 23:43), He sat at the right hand of the Father.

When Jesus said to his apostles, 'I am going to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God' (John 20:17), he clearly referred to his own Father as God, speaking from his human perspective. Through him, we have been called to adoption, and he has given us his Father as our own. Just as we, though called sons of the Father, are still human and have not forgotten the grace of the one who honored us, so too the natural Son and Lord, though he recognized God as his Father through his flesh and his likeness to us, did not cease to be what he is.

The Word of God, who became human through us, anoints his own temple with his own Spirit, not imparting a partial energy, nor in a hierarchical order as he gives to us, but rather filling it with sanctification and his own power and glory. For he said, 'I sanctify myself for their sake, so that they also may be' (John 17:19). We, on the other hand, have been anointed with the Holy Spirit, and by nature, we have been defined as being such, to the extent that the nature of divinity of all created things is understood. How then can it be said that he was anointed apart from those who share in him? Let us consider this question and try to provide an answer.

title: Christ's Divine Superiority Over Angels
english: For indeed, with him nothing is imperishable and indestructible. Moreover, he adds to these points a clear and most evident demonstration of his natural superiority, quoting Scripture: 'To which of the angels did he ever say, Sit at my right hand?' Are not all spirits ministering, sent forth for service on account of those who are about to inherit salvation? For if one who partakes of the divine nature—even if imagined as surrounded by lordly dignity, even if conceived as son of David having taken a body from the holy virgin—yet those who stand present as God and king of all things, to which of the existing beings is the difference lying between Christ and angels invisible? For the one indeed is Son and God, but the others, holding only the measure of servility, reckon that genuine worth consists in obedience to the highest glory; they consider the true to be found in submission, not in innate honor.

But if anyone should say, And who will persuade us in what way one might think him, having been born in the last times of the age through the holy virgin, to have founded the earth at the beginning and themselves to have raised up the heavens, he will receive back from us as if he had chosen to conceive the power of the true union—not the union understood merely in distinct persons or according to will and good pleasure—he will indeed find, through the economy of God, that the human things have come to pass, and that they are not foreign to the divine purpose.
